Issues.Title: [release/11.0] Fix empty PathBase on first IIS in-process request after startup
Issues.Body:
Backport of #69398 to release/11.0

/cc @halter73 @Souheyl7Gouadria

# Fix empty PathBase on first IIS in-process request after startup

Initialize the IIS virtual path before requests can be dispatched.

## Description

`IISHttpServer.StartAsync` registers native callbacks before reading the application's virtual path. Registration enables ANCM to dispatch requests, so a request constructed during that window sees an empty `PathBase` and an unsplit `Path`. For an application deployed at `/myapi`, `/myapi/v1/ping` consequently fails to match the `/v1/ping` endpoint.

Pass `pwzVirtualApplicationPath` through an internal `IISServerOptions` property using the existing native configuration snapshot in `UseIIS()`. The server resolves these options during construction, before callback registration. Remove the redundant native property query from `StartAsync` rather than moving it back before registration, preserving the shutdown-race protection introduced by #60399.

This is an unchanged backport of the three-file fix merged in #69398. It does not include the separate, pre-existing server-address publication issue tracked in #69704.

Fixes #69392

## Customer Impact

ASP.NET Core 10.0 applications hosted in-process under an IIS virtual application path can intermittently return 404 for the request that cold-starts the application, including after deployment or an app-pool idle timeout. Subsequent identical requests route correctly. This can affect any application using that deployment configuration; the reporter observed it in two applications.

The reported workaround uses an `IStartupFilter` and reflection over internal IIS server state to repair the request path before routing. Although it mitigates the failure, it depends on implementation details and requires application changes. Correct framework initialization restores the working 9.0 behavior without requiring that workaround.

## Regression?

- [x] Yes
- [ ] No

Regression from ASP.NET Core 9.0. Commit `512209d2ccd8df506b3c302385fa840ff09d76d7` (#60399) introduced the ordering change during 10.0 development. It is absent from 10.0 Preview 1 and present in Preview 2. The failure was reproduced on 10.0.12; the same controlled startup interleaving succeeds on 9.0.20.

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

The change only moves the source of the virtual-path value into the existing startup configuration-to-options flow. It adds no public API, dependency, native ABI, packaging change, or per-request native call. Request path splitting and native shutdown callbacks are unchanged. Reusing the already-captured native snapshot removes a shutdown-sensitive query instead of reinstating it in the server constructor. The fix has already merged to main.

## Verification

- [x] Manual (required)
- [ ] Automated

## Packaging changes reviewed?

- [ ] Yes
- [ ] No
- [x] N/A

No package, dependency, project, shared-framework composition, or native binary layout changes. The new option is internal.

If faithful test authoring itself is blocked, explain the specific blocker instead of inventing speculative protocol machinery.
> 
> Preserve the current non-draft status. Do not mark ready/draft, merge, close, relabel, request CCR/CI reruns, or work on another issue/PR. Do not assess or discuss security implications. Use GPT models only, with no subagents; report if you cannot honor that. Reply with changed files, exact validation outcomes, and remaining limitations.

Issues.Title: [release/11.0] [SignalR] Bind connection tokens to their endpoint mapping
Issues.Body:
Backport of #69279 to release/11.0

/cc @BrennanConroy @javiercn

# [SignalR] Bind connection tokens to their endpoint mapping

Bind SignalR connection tokens to their originating endpoint mapping.

## Description

Assign each `MapConnections` registration a unique internal mapping identity and retain it on negotiated connections. Token-consuming requests now verify that the selected endpoint has the same identity, so a token negotiated on one mapping cannot be used by another mapping.

This preserves normal same-mapping behavior, including long polling, WebSockets, authentication refresh, and direct WebSocket connections. No public API is added.

Fixes #69090

## Customer Impact

No impact on all supported scenarios, only prevents misuse.

Applications with multiple `MapConnections` registrations now consistently apply the options configured for the mapping that negotiated each connection, rather than accepting its token on a different mapping.

## Regression?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No

## Risk

- [ ] High
- [ ] Medium
- [x] Low

The change is limited to internal connection lookup and endpoint metadata. Coverage verifies that tokens are rejected on an unrelated mapping and continue to work on their originating mapping across normal transport, WebSockets, and authentication-refresh paths.

Issues.Title: Blazor Server: RemoteJSDataStream is orphaned and ends the circuit when sendJSDataStream initiation throws
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

In Blazor Server (.NET 10), `RemoteJSDataStream.CreateRemoteJSDataStreamAsync` constructs and registers the `RemoteJSDataStream`, which starts its no-data timer, **before** it awaits the JS call `Blazor._internal.sendJSDataStream`. If that JS call throws, the exception propagates out of `IJSStreamReference.OpenReadStreamAsync`. The stream that was already registered is never returned to the caller, so the caller has no way to dispose it.

About 60 s later (the JS interop default call timeout) the orphaned stream's timer fires. It raises `System.TimeoutException: Did not receive any data in the allotted time.` as an unhandled circuit exception (`CircuitHost[111]`), and the circuit ends. This happens on a live, healthy connection. The application handled the original exception and the page is otherwise idle.

Disposing the `IJSStreamReference` does not help, because the hidden `RemoteJSDataStream` is a different object, held only in the runtime's registry.

### Expected Behavior

If stream initiation fails, the registered `RemoteJSDataStream` is disposed or unregistered (its timer stopped) before the exception propagates to the caller. A failed `OpenReadStreamAsync` should not end the circuit a minute later.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. In a Blazor Server app, get an `IJSStreamReference` to a `File` (for example a JS function that returns `input.files[0]`), and call `await reference.OpenReadStreamAsync(maxAllowedSize)` inside a `try/catch`.
2. Before the call, make initiation fail in the browser:
   ```js
   const send = Blazor._internal.sendJSDataStream;
   Blazor._internal.sendJSDataStream = async (...args) => { throw new Error("initiation failed (test)"); };
   ```
3. The `OpenReadStreamAsync` call throws a `JSException`. Catch it and dispose the `IJSStreamReference`.
4. Leave the page open and idle for 75 s, then trigger any server round trip (a button click).

Result: about 60 s after step 3 the server logs:

```
fail: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Circuits.CircuitHost[111]
      Unhandled exception in circuit '...'.
      System.TimeoutException: Did not receive any data in the allotted time.
```

The click in step 4 gets no response, because the circuit is gone.

The exception from step 3 has this stack (trimmed):

```
Microsoft.JSInterop.JSException
   at Microsoft.JSInterop.JSRuntime.InvokeAsync[TValue](...)
   at Microsoft.JSInterop.JSRuntimeExtensions.InvokeVoidAsync(...)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Circuits.RemoteJSDataStream.CreateRemoteJSDataStreamAsync(RemoteJSRuntime runtime, IJSStreamReference jsStreamReference, Int64 totalLength, ...)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Server.Circuits.RemoteJSRuntime.ReadJSDataAsStreamAsync(IJSStreamReference jsStreamReference, Int64 totalLength, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
   at Microsoft.JSInterop.Implementation.JSStreamReference.Microsoft.JSInterop.IJSStreamReference.OpenReadStreamAsync(Int64 maxAllowedSize, CancellationToken cancellationToken)
```

The patch in step 2 is only a deterministic way to make initiation fail. In our CI the circuit ended in some runs and survived in others, so the outcome is timing-dependent. A failure of the JS stream itself after initiation (for example a file read error) goes through the normal chunk-error path and does not have this problem.

### Exceptions (if any)

`System.TimeoutException: Did not receive any data in the allotted time.`, raised from `RemoteJSDataStream`'s timeout as an unhandled circuit exception.

### .NET Version

10.0.100 SDK, Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.x

### Anything else?

There is no public API that lets the app release the orphaned stream, and reaching into the runtime's stream registry through reflection is not something we want to ship.

Issues.Title: Avoid SectionRenderModeMismatch warning for PageTitle in default Blazor apps
Issues.Body:
## Description

The default Blazor Web App uses a static `HeadOutlet` with an interactive
`PageTitle` on pages such as Counter. The section render-mode diagnostic
therefore reports a warning during prerendering even though the constant title
is rendered correctly and the page becomes interactive normally.

The warning identifies the built-in section as `System.Object`, which does not
help users determine that the mismatch comes from `PageTitle` and `HeadOutlet`.

This change makes the built-in head-section diagnostics actionable and avoids
emitting a Warning for the expected default-template configuration. A
`PageTitle` mismatch with a static `HeadOutlet` is logged at Debug instead.
Other section render-mode mismatches continue to log at Warning.

---

## Root Cause

`HeadOutlet` uses internal object instances as the identifiers for its title and
head-content sections. When `SectionRegistry` reports a render-mode mismatch,
formatting one of these identifiers produces `System.Object` rather than the
names of the participating components.

In the default per-page interactivity template:

1. `HeadOutlet` is rendered in the static component tree.
2. The Counter page and its `PageTitle` use an interactive render mode.
3. Prerendering connects the title content to the static outlet and displays the
   expected title.
4. The render-mode mismatch diagnostic still logs at Warning because the static
   outlet and interactive title cannot exchange subsequent interactive updates.

For the template's constant page title, this warning is noisy and suggests that
the page is broken even though the title and page interactivity work as
expected.

---

## Output

### Before

The default Counter page emits:

```text
warn: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Sections.SectionRegistry[1]
      The section with ID 'System.Object' has its SectionOutlet in render mode
      'static server-side rendering' and its SectionContent in render mode
      'InteractiveServerRenderMode'.
```

### After

The default static `HeadOutlet` and interactive `PageTitle` mismatch is logged
at Debug, so it no longer produces a warning under the default logging
configuration.

When the diagnostic is enabled, it identifies the section as
`PageTitle/HeadOutlet` and explains that prerendered content may appear
correctly while subsequent interactive updates cannot cross the render-mode
boundary.

Warnings remain enabled for mismatches where suppressing the warning could hide
unexpected behavior, including `HeadContent`, user-defined sections, and a
static `PageTitle` paired with an interactive `HeadOutlet`.

---

## Fix Details

| File | Change |
| --- | --- |
| `src/Components/Components/src/Sections/SectionRegistry.cs` | Introduce descriptive built-in section identifiers, select the mismatch log level based on the section and outlet render mode, and make the diagnostic guidance more actionable. |
| `src/Components/Web/src/Head/HeadOutlet.cs` | Identify the built-in sections as `PageTitle/HeadOutlet` and `HeadContent/HeadOutlet`. |
| `src/Components/Endpoints/test/EndpointHtmlRendererTest.cs` | Cover PageTitle and HeadContent mismatches across Interactive Server, WebAssembly, and Auto render modes and both component discovery orders. |
| `docs/BlazorComponentsGuidance.md` | Document the diagnostic behavior and the limitation around detecting titles that require interactive updates. |

---

## Tests

`EndpointHtmlRendererTest` covers the following scenarios for Interactive
Server, Interactive WebAssembly, and Interactive Auto render modes, with both
outlet-first and content-first rendering:

- A static `HeadOutlet` with an interactive `PageTitle` logs at Debug.
- A static `HeadOutlet` with interactive `HeadContent` continues to log at
  Warning.
- An interactive `HeadOutlet` with a static `PageTitle` continues to log at
  Warning.
- A `HeadOutlet` and `PageTitle` using the same render mode do not log a
  mismatch.
- The prerendered title or head content is still present in the rendered HTML.
- The diagnostic uses the descriptive built-in section identifier and includes
  actionable guidance.

## Test Output

<!-- Replace this comment with the exact validation command, its result, and
red/green evidence. The supplied patch does not include test execution output. -->

---

## Notes

- This change does not enable sections to connect across render-mode
  boundaries.
- Interactive title updates still require `PageTitle` and `HeadOutlet` to use
  compatible render modes.
- The Debug exception applies to all `PageTitle` content paired with a static
  `HeadOutlet`. The section registry cannot currently distinguish a constant
  title from one that will be updated after the page becomes interactive.
- Detecting lost interactive title updates without warning for unchanged
  default-template titles remains a follow-up problem.
- `HeadContent` and user-defined section mismatches are intentionally not
  suppressed.

Fixes #69673

Issues.Title: IIS out-of-process hosting truncates `X-Forwarded-For` when the forwarded value exceeds `USHORT`
Issues.Body:
In ANCM v2 out-of-process hosting, the existing `X-Forwarded-For` value is extended with the client endpoint and written back using a length cast to `USHORT`. When the resulting value exceeds 65,535 bytes, the length wraps and only a truncated prefix is forwarded to Kestrel. ASP.NET Core’s forwarded headers middleware may then process this shortened value as the remote endpoint.

The narrowing conversion occurs in [`forwardinghandler.cpp`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/src/Servers/IIS/AspNetCoreModuleV2/OutOfProcessRequestHandler/forwardinghandler.cpp#L855-L895), where `strTemp.QueryCCH()` is passed to `IHttpRequest::SetHeader` as `static_cast<USHORT>(...)`.

Issues.Title: JsonTranscodingRouteAdapter drops literal constraints from single-segment variables
Issues.Body:
`JsonTranscodingRouteAdapter.Parse` rewrites a single-segment variable without checking whether its pattern is a wildcard or a literal.

For example:

```proto
get: "/v1/items/{resource=public}"
```
is converted to:
```
/v1/items/{resource}
```
instead of preserving `public` as a required literal. As a result, the route matches `/v1/items/anything`, not only `/v1/items/public`.

The `remainingSegmentCount == 1` branch should distinguish `*`, `**`, and literal segments, preserving literal matching while still binding the expected field value.

Issues.Body:
# Add an agent skill for porting browser APIs to Components.Platform

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [ ] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable. (Not applicable. This PR changes only skill files.)
- [ ] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable. (Not applicable.)
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Add an agent skill for porting browser APIs to Components.Platform

## Description

This PR adds `port-components-platform-api`, a skill for AI coding agents. It does not change any product code.

The skill is for porting work in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Platform`. It guides an agent that is asked to wrap one browser API, such as the Cookie Store API, as a typed .NET API. Web Storage from #69305 is its reference implementation. In the review of #69305, the reviewers asked me to move the skill into a separate PR, so here it is.

The skill has two files.

- `.github/skills/port-components-platform-api/SKILL.md` has the workflow and the rules.
- `.github/skills/port-components-platform-api/references/type-mapping.md` has the rules for mapping Web IDL types to .NET.

### Design decisions in this skill

To write this skill, I had to make many design decisions about how to wrap a browser API as a .NET API. I studied each of the following topics and made a decision. The skill files contain the decisions and the reasons behind them, so please see them for the details.

**The skill itself**

- **Purpose.** Should it be a general skill for porting one requested API, or should it also decide the porting order?
- **File layout.** One file, or a main file plus reference Markdown files?
- **Trigger.** Which request wording should trigger it? Should a review request trigger it too?

**Workflow and scope**

- **Design proposal.** Should the agent get agreement on a design proposal before it writes code?
- **Scope within a family.** How much of the types and members should be implemented, and how should deferred and excluded ones be handled?
- **Members that are not Baseline.** Mark them `[Experimental]`, or stop and ask?
- **Events and callbacks from JavaScript to .NET.** Implement them now, or defer them?
- **JavaScript module.** Add one, or use only the JS interop features of .NET 10 and later?

**Public API shape**

- **API shape.** One-to-one with Web IDL, or a more .NET-like shape?
- **Return type.** `ValueTask` or `Task`?
- **API conventions.** Should the skill follow `review-public-api/references/conventions.md`? Which one wins on a conflict?
- **Browser objects that can be missing.** A synchronous property, or an asynchronous getter that returns `null`? How should a call fail when the object is missing?
- **Value checks.** Check values in .NET first, or leave them to the browser?
- **Null members of a dictionary.** Check them in .NET, or leave them to the caller?
- **`CancellationToken`.** Which methods should take one?

**Type mapping**

- **Type names.** Use the Web IDL names as they are, or not? What should happen when a name collides with an existing type?
- **Strings.** Which .NET type should `USVString` map to?
- **Numbers and typedefs.** Map them to the underlying number type, to an existing .NET type such as `DateTimeOffset`, or to a new value object type?
- **Precision above 2^53.** Work around it, or accept it?
- **Sequences.** An array, `List<T>`, `IReadOnlyList<T>`, or `IEnumerable<T>`?
- **Typedefs.** Create a .NET type for a typedef, or not?
- **Dictionaries.** `class` or `record`?
- **Dictionary properties.** `{ get; set; }` or `{ get; init; }`?
- **Required members.** `required` members or constructor parameters?
- **Non-required members of a returned dictionary.** Nullable or not?
- **Members with a default value.** Copy the default into .NET, or make them nullable and leave them out when not set?
- **A missing member versus `null`.** How should serialization tell them apart?
- **Enums.** Convert them to strings with a naming policy, or name each member explicitly?
- **Optional dictionary parameters.** An overload without the parameter, or `= null`?
- **The ambiguous `GetAsync(null)`.** Fix it, or accept it?

**Trimming**

- **Unit of trimming.** Only per family, or per member too?
- **Dictionary members lost from arguments.** Fix a loss after a test finds it, or add `[DynamicDependency]` from the start?

**Disposal**

- **Shared wrappers.** A public `IAsyncDisposable`, an explicit implementation, or an internal interface?
- **Scope of the disposal rule.** Should it also apply to objects that the caller owns?
- **Pending acquisition.** Should disposal wait for it?

**Documentation and tests**

- **XML docs.** How much should be written, and which phrasing should be followed?
- **E2E.** Should the tests prove that every dictionary member makes a round trip in a trimmed WebAssembly app?

Related to #69304 and #69305.

Issues.Title: [Blazor] Cancel LocationChangingContext.CancellationToken only when navigation is superseded
Issues.Body:
## Description

`LocationChangingContext.CancellationToken` was previously signaled whenever navigation processing completed, including successful navigations and navigations prevented via `PreventNavigation()`.

This behavior was inconsistent with the documented purpose of the token, which is to indicate that the associated navigation was canceled. As a result, callbacks registered on the token were invoked even when navigation completed normally.

## Changes

- Updated `NavigationManager.NotifyLocationChangingAsync()` to signal `LocationChangingContext.CancellationToken` only when the navigation is superseded by a subsequent navigation.
- Preserved existing navigation prevention behavior while avoiding unnecessary token cancellation for completed navigations.
- Updated tests to validate the expected cancellation semantics.

## Behavior

| Scenario | CancellationToken Signaled |
|-----------|-----------|
| Successful navigation | No |
| Navigation prevented using `PreventNavigation()` | No |
| Navigation superseded by a newer navigation | Yes |

This aligns the implementation with the documented intent of `LocationChangingContext.CancellationToken` and resolves the issue where cancellation callbacks were invoked for successful navigations.

Fixes #45618

Issues.Title: Kestrel HTTP/1: control characters accepted in header names, chunk extensions, and trailer names; RFC 9110 6.6 forbidden trailer fields stored unfiltered (hardening)
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

Kestrel's HTTP/1 request parsing is materially more lenient than RFC 9110/9112 (and than strict intermediaries such as nginx/HAProxy) in three related areas. All were confirmed live on ASP.NET Core 10.0.12 (loopback lab app, 44-case probe matrix) and source-confirmed against the pinned v10.0.12 tree:

**1. Header names — only NUL and non-ASCII bytes are rejected.** A request header name containing other control characters (e.g. `0x01`) is accepted and reaches the application verbatim via `Request.Headers` (RFC 9110 §5.1 restricts names to `tchar`).

**2. Chunk extensions — content is entirely unvalidated.** `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` chunk-extension values containing control characters or NUL are accepted and skipped (only CRLF-injection sequences are rejected); even a ~65 KB extension is accepted. RFC 9112 §7.1.1 defines a `chunk-ext` token/quoted-string grammar that is not enforced.

**3. Request trailers — names stored verbatim, forbidden fields unfiltered.**
- A trailer name containing control char `0x01` reaches `IHttpRequestTrailersFeature` verbatim (`X\u0001Foo`).
- Fields that RFC 9110 §6.6 forbids in trailers — `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Host`, etc. — are accepted and stored unfiltered: `HttpProtocol.OnTrailer` (`HttpProtocol.cs:546-571`) appends any name/value to the trailer `HeaderDictionary` with no allow/deny list anywhere on the path.
- Duplicate trailers comma-join (`X-Foo: a`, `X-Foo: b` → `a,b`); trailers share the `MaxRequestHeaderCount` budget (exceeding it yields a clean 431).

Mitigating architecture (verified): trailers are kept in a dictionary **separate** from `Request.Headers`, so ASP.NET Core routing, host filtering, and auth never observe them — framework internals are not polluted. No security impact on Kestrel itself was demonstrated. The concern is (a) parser-differential surface: strict intermediaries reject what Kestrel accepts, so Kestrel-behind-a-strict-proxy vs Kestrel-direct can interpret the same bytes differently, and (b) applications/libraries that consume request trailers (integrity checkers, upload pipelines) receive RFC-forbidden fields and control-character names that the spec says must never appear.

### Expected Behavior

- Reject header/trailer names containing bytes outside `tchar` with 400 (RFC 9110 §5.1/§5.6.2), matching Http.Sys and common strict proxies.
- Enforce (or at minimum control-character-filter) the `chunk-ext` grammar of RFC 9112 §7.1.1.
- Discard or reject RFC 9110 §6.6 forbidden fields arriving as trailers (`Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Host`, auth/cache-related fields), or at least document the unfiltered behavior as an application responsibility.

### Steps To Reproduce

Minimal echo app (`dotnet new web`):

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapPost("/echo", async (HttpContext ctx) =>
{
    await ctx.Request.Body.CopyToAsync(Stream.Null);
    var headers = string.Join(";", ctx.Request.Headers.Select(h => $"{h.Key}={h.Value}"));
    var trailers = ctx.Features.Get<IHttpRequestTrailersFeature>() is { } f && f.Trailers != null
        ? string.Join(";", f.Trailers.Select(t => $"{t.Key}={t.Value}")) : "(none)";
    await ctx.Response.WriteAsync($"H[{headers}] T[{trailers}]");
});
app.Run("http://127.0.0.1:5000");
```

Raw-socket payloads (`\x01` = one 0x01 byte; use `printf` with `\001`):

```bash
# 1) control char in a request header NAME -> accepted; app sees X\x01Foo
printf 'POST /echo HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:5000\r\nX-\001Foo: bar\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 5000

# 2) control char + NUL inside a chunk extension -> accepted and skipped
printf 'POST /echo HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:5000\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n5;ext\001val=abc\r\nHello\r\n0\r\n\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 5000

# 3) control-char trailer name + RFC 9110 6.6 forbidden trailer fields -> stored verbatim,
#    visible via IHttpRequestTrailersFeature
printf 'POST /echo HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:5000\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n5\r\nHello\r\n0\r\nX-\001Foo: bar\r\nContent-Length: 999\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\nHost: evil.test\r\n\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 5000
```

All three return `200 OK`, and the echo shows the control-char header/trailer names and the forbidden trailer fields reaching application code.

Controls: NUL (`\x00`) or non-ASCII bytes in a header name → clean 400; CRLF inside a chunk extension → clean 400; trailer count above `MaxRequestHeaderCount` → clean 431.

### Exceptions (if any)

None — all leniencies produce successful 200 responses; the defect is missing validation, not a crash.

### .NET Version

.NET SDK 10.0.100; ASP.NET Core 10.0.12 (Kestrel). Behavior source-confirmed against the v10.0.12 tree (`HttpProtocol.OnHeader`/`OnTrailer`, `Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.ParseChunkExtension` paths); no relevant validation changes identified on `main` as of 2026-10-13.

### Anything else?

- OS: macOS (arm64). Loopback-only testing against a researcher-owned lab app; full 44-case characterization matrix (status + app-visible body assertions) available on request.
- One cross-lane observation offered as a question, not an assertion: `OnTrailer` decodes trailer **values** with `checkForNewlineChars: false`, while request-header value decoding uses `true`. This is inert on HTTP/1 (the wire parser rejects CR/LF in trailer values first), but the same code path is shared with HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, where HPACK/QPACK-encoded values can carry arbitrary bytes — the team may want to confirm raw CR/LF cannot reach apps via H2/H3 trailer values.
- We found no demonstrated security impact within Kestrel itself (framework dictionaries are unpolluted; exposure is bounded to trailer-consuming application code), so this is filed publicly as a **hardening / RFC-conformance** issue per SECURITY.md rather than via MSRC. If the team considers any part security-relevant (e.g. the proxy-differential angle), we are happy to move details to MSRC privately.

Issues.Title: Kestrel HTTP/1: chunk size greater than Int32.MaxValue produces unhandled IOException (OverflowException) and HTTP 500 instead of 400
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

When Kestrel parses an HTTP/1.1 `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` request body and encounters a chunk size that is syntactically valid hex but numerically exceeds `Int32.MaxValue` (e.g. `80000000`, `FFFFFFFF`, `100000000`, `FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`), the result is an unhandled `System.IO.IOException` (inner `System.OverflowException`) surfaced to the application out of `Request.Body.ReadAsync(...)`, rendered as **HTTP 500** with a full server-side stack trace logged.

Root cause (source-confirmed on v10.0.12 and still present on `main`/`release/10.0` as of 2026-10-13): `Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.CalculateChunkSize` (`src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http/Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.cs`) accumulates hex digits into an `int` inside a `checked` block. A non-hex digit correctly throws `KestrelBadHttpRequestException` (`BadChunkSizeData` → clean 400), but the overflow path catches `OverflowException` and rethrows it as a plain `IOException("Bad chunk size data.")`. Since that is not a `BadHttpRequestException`, Kestrel's bad-request→400 mapping never sees it, and the exception escapes through the body-read pipeline into the application/middleware layer → 500 + logged stack trace.

The trigger is fully client-controlled and requires no body data at all — just the chunk-size line. Any endpoint that reads the request body is affected. Characterized behavior around the 500: Kestrel sends `500` with `Content-Length: 0`, then closes the connection; a pipelined successor request is dropped unprocessed; no framing desync or connection-reuse poisoning was observed, and the server stays healthy afterwards.

Impact is robustness/correctness rather than a demonstrated security defect: a client-caused syntax error is reported as a *server* error, pollutes application logs with stack traces (monitoring-noise amplifier), breaks the middleware/app invariant that body-read failures are `BadHttpRequestException`-mapped 400s (or application-level `IOException`s), and in Development environments renders exception details to the client via the Developer Exception Page. Same exception-type-correctness family as the previously fixed `X-Content-Length` `ArgumentException` abort (#65445).

### Expected Behavior

A chunk size exceeding the parser's numeric range should be rejected as a client error — `400 Bad Request` (`BadHttpRequestException` with `BadChunkSizeData`), or `413` where a body-size limit applies — never an unhandled exception / 500. RFC 9112 §7.1 treats invalid chunked coding as a client (4xx-class) error.

### Steps To Reproduce

Minimal app (`dotnet new web`):

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
var app = builder.Build();
app.MapPost("/drain", async (HttpContext ctx) =>
{
    var buf = new byte[8192];
    int total = 0, n;
    while ((n = await ctx.Request.Body.ReadAsync(buf)) > 0) { total += n; }
    await ctx.Response.WriteAsync($"read {total}");
});
app.Run("http://127.0.0.1:5000");
```

Send the request over a raw socket (the overflow is in the size line; no body bytes needed):

```bash
printf 'POST /drain HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: 127.0.0.1:5000\r\nTransfer-Encoding: chunked\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n80000000\r\n' | nc 127.0.0.1 5000
```

Observed: `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error`, with the exception below logged server-side. Same result for `FFFFFFFF`, `100000000`, and `FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF`.

Controls that show the discontinuity is exactly at the Int32 boundary:
- non-hex size (`ZZ`) → clean `400 Bad Request`;
- `7FFFFFFF` (valid size) → no exception; the app waits for body data / `MaxRequestBodySize` applies (413), as expected.

### Exceptions (if any)

```text
System.IO.IOException: Bad chunk size data.
 ---> System.OverflowException: Arithmetic operation resulted in an overflow.
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.Internal.Http.Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.CalculateChunkSize(Int32 extraHexDigit, Int32 currentParsedSize)
   --- End of inner exception stack trace ---
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.Internal.Http.Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.CalculateChunkSize(Int32 extraHexDigit, Int32 currentParsedSize)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.Internal.Http.Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.ParseChunkedPrefix(ReadOnlySequence`1& buffer, SequencePosition& consumed, SequencePosition& examined)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.Internal.Http.Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.Read(...)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.Internal.Http.Http1ChunkedEncodingMessageBody.PumpAsync()
   ... surfaces via HttpRequestStream.ReadAsyncInternal into the application delegate
```

### .NET Version

.NET SDK 10.0.100; ASP.NET Core 10.0.12 (Kestrel). The identical `checked` int accumulation + `IOException`-wrapped `OverflowException` code is present in current `main` and `release/10.0` (source inspection, 2026-10-13), so all supported versions appear affected.

### Anything else?

- OS: macOS (arm64). All testing was loopback-only against a researcher-owned lab app.
- Suggested fix direction: on overflow, throw `KestrelBadHttpRequestException.Throw(BadHttpRequestReason.BadChunkSizeData)` (or accumulate into a `long` and map out-of-range sizes to 400/413) so the existing 400 mapping handles it like every other chunk-size grammar violation.
- Pattern note: `OverflowException` appears in exactly one file across Kestrel's `Internal/Http` parsers (this one); HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 have no equivalent checked-int request-parse paths, so the defect is unique to the HTTP/1 chunk-size parser.
- We assess this as a **non-security robustness defect** (desync/reuse impact was specifically probed and ruled out: connection is closed after the 500, pipelined successor dropped, no framing confusion), which is why it is filed publicly per SECURITY.md. If the team views any aspect as security-relevant, we are happy to move the details to MSRC privately.
- A complete repro harness (32-payload chunked-grammar classification oracle with committed baseline, including the four overflow cases and controls) is available on request; a public repro repo can be published if preferred.

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the OpenID Connect handler validates the signed ID token `auth_time` claim whenever `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge` causes an effective `max_age` value to be sent.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69321 and addresses https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/67462.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

The handler sent `max_age` on the authorization request but did not validate the returned ID token's `auth_time`. Applications relied entirely on the identity provider to honor the request. A missing, malformed, stale, or excessively future `auth_time` did not cause authentication to fail.

### New behavior

When an effective `max_age` is sent, the handler correlates the exact value through protected authorization-transaction state and validates every ID token used by the supported authorization flow after normal token and OpenID Connect protocol validation.

The `auth_time` claim must be an integral, nonnegative OpenID Connect NumericDate. Authentication fails when the claim is missing, malformed, fractional, negative, overflowed, later than the current time plus `OpenIdConnectOptions.TokenValidationParameters.ClockSkew`, or older than `max_age` plus that clock skew. Exact boundaries and values within skew are accepted.

The validation covers authorization-code, implicit, and hybrid flows, including both relevant ID tokens in hybrid flows, and both the default `TokenHandler` path and legacy `SecurityTokenValidator` path. No validation occurs when no `max_age` is configured. In addition to the `MaxAge` properties, applications can configure the parameter through `AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` or `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

OpenID Connect Core requires the authorization server to include `auth_time` when `max_age` is requested and recommends that the relying party validate it. Correlating and checking the signed assertion prevents a missing or nonconforming assertion from silently satisfying an application's configured maximum authentication age.

The guarantee remains limited to the trusted identity provider's signed assertion. ASP.NET Core cannot prove that a particular physical authentication ceremony occurred and cannot protect against a compromised identity provider that signs false data. This change does not revalidate UserInfo, refresh-token redemption, local cookie lifetime, or physical user interaction.

### Recommended action

Ensure that identity providers emit a valid signed `auth_time` and honor the requested `max_age` whenever the application configures that parameter, most commonly through `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge` or `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`.

For a temporarily incompatible provider, restore the previous request-only behavior by setting the process-wide compatibility switch before authentication starts:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch(
    "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation",
    true);
```

The equivalent runtime configuration is:

```json
{
  "runtimeOptions": {
    "configProperties": {
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect.DisableMaxAgeValidation": true
    }
  }
}
```

The switch defaults to `false` and is intended only as a temporary provider-compatibility escape hatch.

When pushed authorization is used, set or modify `max_age` in `OnRedirectToIdentityProvider`. Changing it later in `OnPushAuthorization` is rejected while validation is active unless pushing is skipped, because the handler has already correlated the value with the authorization response.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. The behavioral change affects applications that set:

- `OpenIdConnectOptions.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectChallengeProperties.MaxAge`
- `OpenIdConnectOptions.AdditionalAuthorizationParameters` when it includes `max_age`
- `OpenIdConnectEvents.OnRedirectToIdentityProvider` when it sets `max_age`
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "[Breaking change]: OpenID Connect max_age validates auth_time" (#537)

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Identity external login keys use ordinal equality
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, the built-in Entity Framework Core Identity stores verify external-login `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values using managed ordinal equality after the indexed database lookup returns a candidate.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/69277.

### Version

.NET 11 RC 2

### Previous behavior

`UserStore` and `UserOnlyStore` filtered external logins with a database-translated equality predicate. The database collation therefore determined whether the stored `(LoginProvider, ProviderKey)` tuple matched the supplied values.

On a case-insensitive collation, `FindByLoginAsync` could resolve a login whose provider name or provider key differed only by case. On databases where equality ignores trailing spaces, it could also resolve a key that differed by trailing spaces. `RemoveLoginAsync` used the same collation-dependent lookup and could remove such a login.

### New behavior

The database equality remains the indexed candidate lookup. The built-in EF Identity stores then require the returned `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` to match the requested values using `StringComparison.Ordinal`.

A collation-only match now causes `FindByLoginAsync` to return no user and `RemoveLoginAsync` to perform no removal. Exact ordinal matches continue to work.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

External provider keys are opaque identifiers whose equality must not vary with the configured database provider or collation. Managed ordinal verification makes the built-in EF stores consistent with the in-memory reference store while preserving the existing indexed database lookup.

### Recommended action

Ensure that applications persist and later supply the exact `LoginProvider` and `ProviderKey` values issued for an external login. Do not normalize, case-fold, trim, or otherwise alter provider keys.

Third-party `IUserLoginStore<TUser>` implementations own their equality semantics. Implementations that query a collation-aware database should preserve an indexed candidate lookup and verify the materialized provider name and key with ordinal equality before resolving or removing a login.

### Affected APIs

No public API signatures change. This behavioral change affects the built-in Entity Framework Core implementations of:

- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.FindByLoginAsync`
- `IUserLoginStore<TUser>.RemoveLoginAsync`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Blazor server-side rendering defers antiforgery validation to middleware
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 11, Blazor static server-side rendering (SSR) endpoints no longer validate antiforgery tokens themselves. They rely on the antiforgery verdict recorded by upstream middleware and generate antiforgery tokens only when token-based antiforgery middleware is present.

This change was introduced by https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/67082.

### Version

.NET 11 Preview 6

### Previous behavior

When a Blazor SSR endpoint handled a form `POST`, the endpoint validated the request itself if antiforgery middleware hadn't already recorded a result.

The endpoint also generated and stored antiforgery tokens for rendered forms even when `app.UseAntiforgery()` wasn't present in the pipeline.

Consequently, apps that didn't call `app.UseAntiforgery()` still emitted and validated antiforgery tokens.

### New behavior

Blazor SSR endpoints now trust the `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature` verdict recorded by upstream middleware. A form `POST` is rejected with `400 Bad Request` when the recorded verdict is invalid.

The verdict can be recorded by:

- Token-based antiforgery middleware added by `app.UseAntiforgery()` (explicit usage).
- Automatic cross-origin CSRF protection middleware added by default to apps built with `WebApplication.CreateBuilder`.

Blazor SSR endpoints no longer call `IAntiforgery.ValidateRequestAsync` directly. Antiforgery tokens are generated only when token-based antiforgery middleware ran for the request.

Apps using `app.UseAntiforgery()` retain token-based validation. Apps without it rely on automatic cross-origin CSRF protection and no longer emit antiforgery tokens for their forms.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Token-based antiforgery and automatic cross-origin CSRF protection now record a shared verdict through `IAntiforgeryValidationFeature`.

Validating again inside the Blazor SSR endpoint duplicated work and could produce a result different from the middleware verdict. Generating tokens without token-based antiforgery middleware also produced tokens that nothing validated.

### Recommended action

If your Blazor SSR app relies on antiforgery tokens for form validation or rendering, ensure that it calls `app.UseAntiforgery()`:
```csharp
var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAntiforgery();
```

If you were not calling `app.UseAntiforgery()` before you will start using CSRF protection as the defense mechanism from now on.

### Affected APIs

None. This is a behavioral change affecting Blazor SSR form processing and antiforgery-token generation.

# ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach end of support on April 13, 2027

Today we are announcing that ASP.NET Core 2.3 will reach **end of support on April 13, 2027**. After that date, Microsoft will no longer provide security patches, bug fixes, or technical support for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

This announcement provides the required 12 months of advance notice, as defined by the [Microsoft Support Lifecycle Policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/lifecycle/faq/general-lifecycle#what-is-the-lifecycle-policy-for-tools-) for products classified as "Tools."

After April 13, 2027, this support will end regardless of the .NET Framework version in use.

Note that the [ASP.NET Core 2.3 packages](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/en-us/platform/support/policy/aspnet/2.3-packages) include the Entity Framework 2.3 packages, which will end support on the same date.

- Technical support will no longer be available for ASP.NET Core 2.3.

We recommend upgrading to a [currently supported version of .NET](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet), such as .NET 10 (LTS).

# Deprecation of Microsoft ASP.NET WebHooks

[Microsoft ASP.NET WebHooks](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/webhooks/) provided support for sending and receiving WebHooks in ASP.NET 4.x applications on .NET Framework 4.5. The project has been in maintenance mode for several years with no planned feature work.

Automates creation of documentation tracking issues in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs` when breaking change issues are opened or labeled in this repository.

**New workflow:** `.github/workflows/create-docs-issue.yaml`

Multi-layer detection to handle race conditions and partial failures:
- Checks for existing bot comments in source issue
- Searches docs repo by title before creating

Separate try-catch blocks for each operation:
- Comment listing failures → proceed with search

- Comment posting failures → don't fail workflow (docs issue already created)
- Permission errors → explicit message about `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` requirement

Configure `DOCS_ISSUE_TOKEN` repository secret with `repo` scope for cross-repository issue creation. Falls back to `GITHUB_TOKEN` but will fail with clear error message.

Explicit minimal permissions: `issues: write`, `contents: read`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Deprecating WebHostBuilder,  IWebHost, and WebHost
Issues.Body:
### Description

`WebHostBuilder` was replaced by `HostBuilder` ([generic host](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder)) in 3.0 and we also added [`WebApplicationBuilder`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) in 6.0.

We are now marking `WebHostBuilder` as obsolete to encourage users to move on to the alternatives which is where future investments will occur, and we're also marking `IWebHost` and `WebHost` as deprecated to clean up other parts of the now obsolete web host story.

### Version

.NET 10 RC 1

### Previous behavior

```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

### New behavior

Using `WebHostBuilder` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR004**:
> warning ASPDEPR004: WebHostBuilder is deprecated in favor of HostBuilder and WebApplicationBuilder. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/004.

Using `IWebHost` or `WebHost` will produce a compiler warning with diagnostic ID **ASPDEPR008**:
> warning ASPDEPR008: WebHost is obsolete. Use HostBuilder or WebApplicationBuilder instead. For more information, visit https://aka.ms/aspnet/deprecate/008.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [x] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [ ] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

We recommend the use of `HostBuilder` and `WebApplication` going forward over `WebHostBuilder` because they have all the features of `WebHostBuilder` and will be the focus of future investment.

### Recommended action

See https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host or https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/minimal-apis/webapplication for more details on the different hosting models. As well as [HostBuilder replaces WebHostBuilder](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/22-to-30#hostbuilder-replaces-webhostbuilder) and [Introducing WebApplication](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/migration/50-to-60#new-hosting-model) for migration guides.

Below is an example of converting `WebHostBuilder` to `HostBuilder`:

**Before**
```csharp
var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
    .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
    .UseStartup()
    .UseKestrel();
// Test code might use TestServer:
var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
```

**After**
```csharp
using var host = new HostBuilder()
    .ConfigureWebHost(webHostBuilder =>
    {
        webHostBuilder
            .UseTestServer() // If using TestServer
            .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
            .UseStartup()
            .UseKestrel();
    })
    .Build();
await host.StartAsync();

var testServer = host.GetTestServer();
```

Both Copilot and ChatGpt have given good results so far when asked to convert a WebHostBuilder example to use HostBuilder. Below is an example prompt:
<details>
<summary>Example AI Prompt</summary>

> Can you convert
>
> var hostBuilder = new WebHostBuilder()
>     .UseContentRoot(Directory.GetCurrentDirectory())
>     .UseStartup()
>     .UseKestrel();
> // Test code might use TestServer:
> var testServer = new TestServer(hostBuilder);
>
> to use HostBuilder.

</details>

### Affected APIs

`public class Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.WebHostBuilder`
`public interface Microsoft.AspNetCore.Hosting.IWebHost`
`public static class Microsoft.AspNetCore.WebHost`

### Discussion

https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/discussions/63480

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Exception diagnostics are suppressed when `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns true
Issues.Body:
### Description

The [ASP.NET Core exception handler middleware](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#exception-handler-page), `UseExceptionHandler()`, is responsible for catching and processing unhandled exceptions from ASP.NET Core requests.

In .NET 8, we introduced [`IExceptionHandler`](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/fundamentals/error-handling#iexceptionhandler). Implementations of `IExceptionHandler` are registered with dependency injection and invoked by the middleware. An implementation can return `true` from `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` to indicate that the exception has been handled. The middleware stops processing the exception once it has been handled.

In .NET 10, we're changing the default behavior so that the middleware no longer records diagnostics for exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

### Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

### Previous behavior

The exception handler middleware recorded diagnostics about exceptions handled by `IExceptionHandler`.

The exception diagnostics are:

- Logging `UnhandledException` to `ILogger`.
- Writing the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HandledException` event to `EventSource`.
- Adding the `error.type` tag to the `http.server.request.duration` metric.

### New behavior

If `IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync` returns `true`, then exception diagnostics are no longer recorded by default.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

ASP.NET Core users have given feedback that the previous behavior was undesirable. Their `IExceptionHandler` implementation reported that the exception was handled, but the error handling middleware still recorded the error in the app's telemetry.

We are changing ASP.NET Core to follow the behavior expected by users by suppressing diagnostics when `IExceptionHandler` handles the exception. We're also adding configuration options to customize exception diagnostics behavior if needed.

### Recommended action

If you want handled exceptions to continue recording telemetry, you can use the new `ExceptionHandlerOptions.SuppressDiagnosticsCallback` option:

```cs
app.UseExceptionHandler(new ExceptionHandlerOptions
{
    SuppressDiagnosticsCallback = context => false;
});
```

The context passed to the callback includes information about the exception, the request, and whether the exception was handled. Returning `false` from the callback indicates that diagnostics shouldn't be suppressed. This restores the previous behavior.

### References

- Issue: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/54554
- PR: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/59074

### Affected APIs

- `UseExceptionHandler()`
- `IExceptionHandler`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and MVC API analyzers are deprecated
Issues.Body:
## Description

The `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` MSBuild property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release. When `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will now emit warning `ASPDEPR007`.

## Version

.NET 10 Preview 7

## Previous behavior

Previously, developers could set `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` in their Web SDK projects to enable MVC API analyzers without any warnings or deprecation notices.

```xml
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net9.0</TargetFramework>
    <IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>
  </PropertyGroup>
</Project>
```

The project would build successfully without any deprecation warnings.

## New behavior

Starting in .NET 10 Preview 7, when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is set to `true`, the build will emit warning `ASPDEPR007`:

```
warning ASPDEPR007: The IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers property and its associated MVC API analyzers are deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
```

The analyzers will continue to function, but developers will receive this deprecation warning during compilation.

## Type of breaking change

- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

## Reason for change

## Reason for change

The MVC API analyzers were originally introduced to help keep return types and attributes in sync for API controllers, ensuring consistency between method signatures and their corresponding OpenAPI documentation. These analyzers provided compile-time validation to catch mismatches between declared return types and the actual types returned by controller actions.

However, with the introduction of Minimal APIs and the `TypedResults` pattern, the .NET ecosystem has evolved toward a more type-safe approach for API development. `TypedResults` provides compile-time guarantees about response types without requiring additional analyzers, making the MVC API analyzers redundant for modern .NET applications. In .NET 10, `TypedResults` are supported in controller-based APIs.

**Previous approach with MVC API analyzers:**
```csharp
[HttpGet]
[ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)]
[ProducesResponseType(404)]
public async Task<ActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    if (product == null)
        return NotFound(); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType(404)
    
    return Ok(product); // Analyzer ensures this matches ProducesResponseType<Product>(200)
}
```

**Or with controller actions using TypedResults:**
```csharp
[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _productService.GetByIdAsync(id);
    return product == null 
        ? TypedResults.NotFound() 
        : TypedResults.Ok(product);
}
```

The `TypedResults` pattern eliminates the need for separate analyzers because the return type itself (`Results<Ok<Product>, NotFound>`) explicitly declares all possible response types at compile time. This approach is more maintainable, provides better IntelliSense support, and automatically generates accurate OpenAPI documentation without additional tooling.

As the .NET ecosystem continues to embrace `TypedResults` as the recommended pattern for API development, the MVC API analyzers have become obsolete and are being deprecated to streamline the development experience.

## Recommended action

Developers should:

1. **Remove the deprecated property**: Remove `<IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>true</IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers>` from your project files to eliminate the warning.

2. **Suppress the warning temporarily**: If you need to continue using the deprecated analyzers temporarily, you can suppress the warning:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ASPDEPR007</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

3. **Migrate to TypedResults**: Migrate to the `TypedResults` pattern documented above to ensure better consistency between application behavior and OpenAPI documentation.

## Affected APIs

- MSBuild property: `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers`
- Associated MVC API analyzers included when `IncludeOpenAPIAnalyzers` is `true`

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Forwarded Headers Middleware Now Ignores X-Forwarded-* Headers from Unknown Proxies
Issues.Body:
### Description

Starting in ASP.NET Core 8.0.17 and 9.0.6, the Forwarded Headers Middleware will ignore all `X-Forwarded-*` headers from proxies that are not explicitly configured as trusted.

### Version

.NET 8

### Previous behavior

Previously, the middleware, when not configured to use `X-Forwarded-For`, would process `X-Forwarded-Prefix`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, and `X-Forwarded-Host` headers from any source, potentially allowing malicious or misconfigured proxies/clients to spoof these headers and affect your application's understanding of client information.

### New behavior

With this change, only headers sent by known, trusted proxies (as configured via `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies` and `ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownNetworks`) will be processed. Headers from unknown sources will be ignored.

**This is a breaking change**: If your deployment relied on forwarded headers from proxies not configured in your application's trusted proxy list, those headers will no longer be honored.

This can cause behavior like infinite redirects if you're using the Https redirection middleware and using TLS termination in your proxy. Or authentication to fail if using TLS termination and expecting an https request.


### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [x] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The change was made for security hardening, as the proxy and IP lists weren't being applied in all cases.

### Recommended action

- **Review your deployment topology:**  
  Ensure that all legitimate proxy servers in front of your app are properly added to `KnownProxies` or `KnownNetworks` in your `ForwardedHeadersOptions` configuration.
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownProxies = { IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_PROXY_IP") }
  });
  ```
  Or, for a network:
  ```csharp
  app.UseForwardedHeaders(new ForwardedHeadersOptions
  {
      KnownNetworks = { new IPNetwork(IPAddress.Parse("YOUR_NETWORK_IP"), PREFIX_LENGTH) }
  });
  ```

- **If you wish to enable previous behavior:**  
  You may need to relax your configuration, but this is **not recommended** due to security risks. You can do this by clearing the `KnownNetworks` and `KnownProxies` lists in `ForwardedHeadersOptions` to allow any proxy or network to forward these headers.

You can also set the `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` environment variable to true, which clears the lists and enables `ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedFor | ForwardedHeaders.XForwardedProto`.

For applications targeting .NET 9.0 or less, you can set the `Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpOverrides.IgnoreUnknownProxiesWithoutFor` [AppContext](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/fundamentals/runtime-libraries/system-appcontext) switch to `"true"` or `1` to get back to the previous behavior. Alternatively, set the `MICROSOFT_ASPNETCORE_HTTPOVERRIDES_IGNORE_UNKNOWN_PROXIES_WITHOUT_FOR` environment variable.

> [!Note]
> In cloud environments, the proxy IP(s) can change over the lifetime of the app and `ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED` is sometimes used to make forwarded headers work.

### References

- [Forwarded Headers Middleware documentation](https://learn.microsoft.com/aspnet/core/host-and-deploy/proxy-load-balancer)

### Affected APIs

`UseForwardedHeaders();`

### Previous behavior

```
dotnet dev-certs https -ep C:\NonExistent\cert.pfx
```

If `C:\NonExistent\` did not exist when the command was run, it would be created (with permissions inherited from the containing directory).

### New behavior

The target directory must exist or the export will fail with a message like `There was an error exporting the HTTPS developer certificate to a file.`

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The development certificate is exported with its private key, so unauthorized access can be very problematic.  It may, nevertheless, be necessary to make it readable to multiple accounts - e.g. if the consuming process will not be run as the current user.  Rather than attempting to determine (and securely establish) permissions for the target directory, `dotnet dev-certs` require that it already exist.

### Recommended action

Create the target directory (with appropriate permissions) before invoking `dotnet dev-certs`.

### Affected APIs

This functionality is not presently exposed via an API - it is invoked from the command line.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Handling of middleware types with multiple constructors
Issues.Body:
### Description

Formerly, when a middleware type with multiple satisfiable constructors was instantiated from the dependency injection container, the one with the most parameters would be used.  Now that only happens if the dependency injection container implements [`IServiceProviderIsService`](https://learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/api/microsoft.extensions.dependencyinjection.iserviceproviderisservice).

### Version

.NET 9 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Formerly, the first constructor was preferred (when both were satisfied) because it has more parameters.

```csharp
public class CookiePolicyMiddleware
{
    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options, ILoggerFactory factory)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }

    public CookiePolicyMiddleware(RequestDelegate next, IOptions<CookiePolicyOptions> options)
    {
        // Omitted for brevity
    }
}
```

### New behavior

Now, neither constructor is preferred and construction fails with an error like 
```
System.InvalidOperationException: 'Multiple constructors accepting all given argument types have been found in type 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware'. There should only be one applicable constructor.'
```

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

The activation mechanism was [changed](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/pull/55722) to help support keyed dependency injection.

### Recommended action

If this happens and you can't upgrade to a dependency injection container that implements `IServiceProviderIsService`, you can add `ActivatorUtilitiesConstructorAttribute` to the preferred constructor of the affected middleware type.

### Affected APIs

This is [known](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/57231) to cause errors when instantiating `Microsoft.AspNetCore.CookiePolicy.CookiePolicyMiddleware` with [Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Autofac.Extensions.DependencyInjection) 7.x.

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey has a slightly altered meaning
Issues.Body:
### Description

`DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey` no longer reflects whether the default key is close to its expiration time.

### Version

.NET 9 Preview 3

### Previous behavior

It was an undocumented, but consistent, feature of the API that `ShouldGenerateNewKey` would be true if the default key was within two days (an over-simplification) of its expiration time.  The amount of lead time was based on the polling interval of `ICacheableKeyRingProvider`, which was not something `IDefaultKeyResolver.ResolveDefaultKeyPolicy` should have depended upon (since, for example, alternative implementations would probably not be aware of these details).

### New behavior

If `ShouldGenerateNewKey` is true, it now indicates that either there is no default key or that for some other policy reason (i.e. in a specialized implementation of `IDefaultKeyResolver`, a new key should be generated.  The `ICacheableKeyRingProvider` will make its own decision about whether the expiration time is close enough to warrant generating a new key.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

First, we wanted to change the logic around key generation near expiration time and, second, this makes it more straightforward to implement a custom `IDefaultKeyResolver`.

Note that the documentation for this type already states that "This API supports infrastructure and is not intended to be used directly from your code. This API may change or be removed in future releases."

### Recommended action

If you have an `IDefaultKeyResolver` implementation that tries to replicate the expiry logic, that logic can be removed (however, leaving it is fine as well).

If you were consuming `IDefaultKeyResolver` directly, for the express purpose of determining whether expiration was pending and that continues to be important, you can the default key's `ExpirationDate` property directly.

### Affected APIs

Microsoft.AspNetCore.DataProtection.KeyManagement.Internal.DefaultKeyResolution.ShouldGenerateNewKey

Issues.Title: [Breaking change]: Minimal APIs consuming IFormFile or IFormFileCollection parameters require anti-forgery checks
Issues.Body:
### Description

Minimal API endpoints that consume an `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` will now be opted-in to requiring anti-forgery token validation using the new anti-forgery middleware.

### Version

.NET 8 RC 1

### Previous behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did not require anti-forgery validation.

### New behavior

Minimal API endpoints that bound a parameter from the form via `IFormFile` or `IFormFileCollection` did require anti-forgery validation. An exception will be thrown if the anti-forgery middleware is not registered for an API that defines these input types.

### Type of breaking change

- [ ] **Binary incompatible**: Existing binaries may encounter a breaking change in behavior, such as failure to load or execute, and if so, require recompilation.
- [ ] **Source incompatible**: When recompiled using the new SDK or component or to target the new runtime, existing source code may require source changes to compile successfully.
- [X] **Behavioral change**: Existing binaries may behave differently at run time.

### Reason for change

Anti-forgery token validation is a recommended security precaution for APIs that consume data from a form.

### Recommended action

Users can opt out of anti-forgery validation for specific endpoints by using the `DisableAntiforgery` method like so:

```csharp
var app = WebApplication.Create();

app.MapPost("/", (IFormFile formFile) => ...)
  .DisableAntiforgery();

app.Run();
```

### Affected APIs

None.
